title: What If You SHRANK to the Size of an Ant?
description:
Glint, 19, works nights at the city science museum. One evening, while cleaning the lens of an old brass projector in the new Tiny Giants exhibit, the beam turns violet and he shrinks to two centimetres tall. Lifting a sugar cube is easy and falling off the table is the best fun he's had in years, but a drop of tea can trap him, and his voice is now too high for Nan to hear. Then Nan dozes off while a pan of oil starts to smoke, and the only one in the house who can hear Glint is the grumpy old cat. The real science of being small (the square-cube law, surface tension, terminal velocity and hearing) is the only thing that can save her.

Would you want to be ant-sized, knowing the people you love might never hear your voice? Tell me in the comments 👇

▶ More What Ifs: What If You NEVER Needed Sleep?

CHAPTERS
0:00 Cold open: Nan can't hear him
0:22 Let's go back: The Tiny Giants projector
1:11 The Rules: The square-cube law
2:08 Plus: Lifting a sugar cube
2:37 Minus: Trapped in a drop of tea (surface tension)
3:11 Plus: Falling is fun (terminal velocity)
3:51 Minus: Voices (deep, slow, and Nan can't hear his)
4:36 Minus: Cold, hunger, and Mr. Pickles
5:23 The Crisis: The smoking pan
6:44 The Solution: Squeak, jump, run
8:21 The Twist: Mr. Pickles was guarding him
9:03 Would you?

SOURCES
• Galileo Galilei, Two New Sciences (1638); Schmidt-Nielsen, Scaling: Why Is Animal Size So Important? (1984): the square-cube law
• Hölldobler & Wilson, The Ants (1990); Nguyen et al., Journal of Biomechanics 47 (2014): ants carrying many times their body weight
• Bush & Hu, "Walking on water: biolocomotion at the interface", Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics 38 (2006); Vogel, Life in Moving Fluids: surface tension and small animals
• J. B. S. Haldane, "On Being the Right Size" (1926); Vogel, Comparative Biomechanics: falling, air resistance and terminal velocity
• Titze, Principles of Voice Production: smaller vocal folds, higher pitch
• Healy et al., "Metabolic rate and body size are linked with perception of temporal information", Animal Behaviour 86 (2013)
• NIDCD (NIH), "Age-Related Hearing Loss": high frequencies are lost first
• ITU-T G.711 / standard telephony references: narrowband phone calls carry about 300–3,400 Hz
• Schmidt-Nielsen, Animal Physiology: body size, heat loss and metabolism (shrews)
• Heffner & Heffner, "Hearing range of the domestic cat", Hearing Research 19 (1985)
• NFPA, "Cooking safety"; London Fire Brigade cooking-fire guidance: smoking oil, pan fires, lids and never water
• Bradshaw, Cat Sense: mother cats carry kittens by the scruff
• Story is fiction: the projector, Glint's working brain and his sped-up brain are made up; the science rules are real.
